decision.explanation: Since x'(t)=9, integration gives x(t)=9t+C. The condition x(1)=0 implies C=-9, so x(t)=9t-9.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=9,$ where $t$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=0$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
after.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 9\,\text{d}t \\  & =9t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $x(1)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =9(1)+C \\ C & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=9t-9.
$$

decision.explanation: Integrating x'(t)=cos(4t) gives x(t)=(1/4)sin(4t)+C. Since x(0)=3 and sin(0)=0, C=3, which matches option a.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),$ where $t$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=3$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
after.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(0))+C \\ 3 & =0+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
x(t)=3+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=\frac{4}{(t+1)^{3}}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=1$ and velocity $v=-\frac{1}{2}$ when $t=1$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
after.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{4}{(t+1)^{3}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{2}{(t+1)^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=-\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{2}{(1+1)^{2}}+C \\ -\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{1}{2}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=-\frac{2}{(t+1)^{2}}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-\frac{2}{(t+1)^{2}})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{t+1}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(1)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{2}{1+1}+K \\ 1 & =1+K \\ K & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{2}{t+1}.
$$

Question 3

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration a(t)=4(t+1)3, where t≥0 is the time. If the particle has position x=1 and velocity v=−12 when t=1, calculate the position x of the particle at time t>0.

a
x(t)=2t+1−1
b
x(t)=1t+1+12
c
x(t)=2t+1
d
x(t)=2(t+1)2
e
x(t)=4(t+1)2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity v(t):

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫4(t+1)3dt=−2(t+1)2+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(1)=−12. Substituting this into the above gives

−12=−2(1+1)2+C−12=−12+CC=0.

So the velocity is given by v(t)=−2(t+1)2.

Now, we integrate the velocity to get x(t):

x(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫(−2(t+1)2)dt=2t+1+K

To determine K, we use the fact that x(1)=1. Substituting this into the above gives

1=21+1+K1=1+KK=0.

Therefore, the position x of the particle at time t is x(t)=2t+1.

content.knowledge_point: Determining the Position of a Particle Given Its Acceleration, Initial Velocity and Initial Position
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=\frac{4}{(t+1)^{3}}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=1$ and velocity $v=-\frac{1}{2}$ when $t=1$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
content.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{4}{(t+1)^{3}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{2}{(t+1)^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=-\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{2}{(1+1)^{2}}+C \\ -\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{1}{2}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=-\frac{2}{(t+1)^{2}}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-\frac{2}{(t+1)^{2}})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{t+1}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(1)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{2}{1+1}+K \\ 1 & =1+K \\ K & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{2}{t+1}.
$$

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration a(t)=cos⁡(4t), where t≥0 is the time. If the particle has position x=116 and velocity v=14 when t=π8, calculate the position x of the particle at time t>0.

a
x(t)=116(1−cos⁡(4t))
b
x(t)=116(2−sin⁡(4t))
c
x(t)=116(1−2cos⁡(4t))
d
x(t)=116(1+sin⁡(4t))
e
x(t)=116(2+cos⁡(4t))
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating acceleration gives v(t)=(1/4)sin(4t)+C. At t=pi/8, sin(4t)=1, so C=0. Integrating again gives x(t)=-(1/16)cos(4t)+K. Since cos(pi/2)=0 and x(pi/8)=1/16, K=1/16. Thus option a is correct.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=\frac{1}{16}$ and velocity $v=\frac{1}{4}$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{8}$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
after.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{8})=\frac{1}{4}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})+C \\ \frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(\frac{\pi }{8})=\frac{1}{16}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16} & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})+C \\ \frac{1}{16} & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{16} & =0+C \\ K & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=\frac{1}{16}$ and velocity $v=\frac{1}{4}$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{8}$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
content.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{8})=\frac{1}{4}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})+C \\ \frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(\frac{\pi }{8})=\frac{1}{16}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16} & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})+C \\ \frac{1}{16} & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{16} & =0+C \\ K & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$
